data.title: Wall Street warns: Jensen Huang's departure could trigger an "AI-driven quantitative tightening"
data.description:
Author: Zhang Yaqi, Wall Street Insights

The sudden departure of Jensen Huang has left Nvidia's over $500 billion AI revolving financing machine, built on equity investments, guarantees, and buybacks, without its operator. Goldman Sachs and UBS warn that a large portion of its quarterly free cash flow is recycled back to customers and suppliers, and even a temporary halt could withdraw more than $50 billion, essentially triggering "AI quantitative tightening," with emerging cloud service providers bearing the brunt of the impact.

Nvidia Chairman Jensen Huang's sudden departure is not just a change in executives at a chip company, but a systemic shock to the entire AI financing ecosystem. Over the past three years, Nvidia has effectively become the "lender of last resort" in the AI ​​industry, building a revolving financing machine of over $500 billion through equity investments, guarantees, and buyback agreements. Now, the operator of this machine has left.

... Following the announcement of Jensen Huang's resignation, Nvidia's stock price plummeted by over 13% intraday, closing down about 4%. Simultaneously, 14 sell-side institutions, including Goldman Sachs, UBS, and William Blair, downgraded their ratings or target prices, all pointing to the same core concern: can Nvidia continue to provide funding for the AI ​​ecosystem without Huang? Neocloud, an emerging cloud service provider reliant on Nvidia's funding, reacted even more strongly—CoreWeave (CRWV) fell 11% that day, while on the same day, the company was marketing a more than $4 billion investment-grade loan, for which Nvidia is reportedly the guarantor. CFO Colette Kress assumed the role of interim CEO while also serving as CFO. The core question facing Wall Street is no longer Nvidia's performance in the next fiscal quarter, but rather: after this company's "brain transplant," will the financing machine that provides credit backing for the entire AI industry continue to operate normally? Selling chips, funding buyers, and bailing out landlords: Nvidia's $530 billion cycle. Nvidia's financing landscape is far larger than most investors realize. As of July 26th this year, Nvidia held $99 billion in equity investments, approximately 13 times the amount a year ago; in addition, it has $108.5 billion in guarantee commitments, and $56 billion in AI cloud buyback agreements and third-party leases. This investment list is practically a roster of Nvidia's own customers and suppliers: In terms of AI labs, Nvidia invested $30 billion in OpenAI in March, up to $10 billion in Anthropic, and about $5 billion in Safe Superintelligence in July; in terms of emerging cloud service providers, Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January and prepaid $2 billion in warrants for Nebius in March; in terms of the supply chain, Nvidia invested $5 billion in Intel (currently valued at about $30 billion), and also invested $2 billion each in Coherent, Lumentum, Marvell, and Synopsys. The operational structure remains almost unchanged: Nvidia buys equity, the investee promises to purchase Nvidia hardware, and the funds flow back in the form of GPU orders. Taking the OpenAI Ohio campus project as an example, Nvidia's guarantee is capped at $105 billion, with an option for an additional 3.8 gigawatts of computing power. Nvidia's own CFO's commentary clarifies the return logic: each generation of Nvidia infrastructure deployment at this site corresponds to approximately 1.5 million GPUs, equivalent to approximately $150 billion to $200 billion in Nvidia revenue—in other words, Nvidia uses $105 billion in rental guarantees in exchange for potential chip revenue of up to $200 billion per upgrade cycle, a cycle spanning up to 20 years. Adding up all the commitments in the footnotes of Nvidia's 10-Q report yields the following figures: $366 billion in future commitments (of which $279 billion are for supply and capacity procurement, a surge from $119 billion in just three months), $56 billion in "additional" commitments, and $108.5 billion in guarantees—totaling $530.5 billion. This does not include $99 billion in equity book value, or the portion of the $500 billion financing platform launched by Jensen Huang in August of this year with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, for which Nvidia has committed to provide up to 25% of the guarantee, or $125 billion. Regarding the essence of this financing machine, Panmure Liberum once pointed out incisively: the so-called "Nvidia Bank" is both the chip company's moat and the credit risk accumulated from the massive betting of limited free cash flow on an industry still struggling to find a way to monetize. Goldman Sachs and UBS have successively warned of the transmission path of "AI-based quantitative tightening." After Jensen Huang's departure, Wall Street's focus has quickly shifted from Nvidia itself to the chain reaction of its financing contraction on the entire AI ecosystem. Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider maintained a buy rating but lowered his price target from $300 to $220. In his report, he wrote: "Nvidia's existing commitments will be fulfilled; the question is the next round. Without Jensen Huang's personal vision, network, and rallying power, new multi-party ecosystem investments will be more difficult to advance." Goldman Sachs also pointed out that Nvidia stock had already been trading at a significant discount, partly because the market was pricing in a "sudden slowdown in AI infrastructure growth after vendor financing stopped." UBS analyst Tim Arcuri, in his preliminary analysis released that evening, listed financing issues as the top of the three core impacts. He estimated that a significant portion of Nvidia's approximately $50-60 billion in free cash flow each quarter is recycled back to customers, vendors, and emerging cloud service providers. Even a temporary pause could potentially draw more than $50 billion from the AI ​​ecosystem at a critical moment—equivalent to an "AI quantitative tightening" triggered by a press release. William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji downgraded Nvidia to "market performance," concluding that while existing contracts are unaffected by the CEO change, the next round of deals is precarious, directly impacting Nvidia's ability to maintain market share in 2027 and beyond. Meanwhile, competitors like Broadcom are poised to capitalize on this vulnerability—Broadcom has already provided guarantees of up to 72.5% for two chip financing deals for Anthropic, while Nvidia's financing platform only offers a maximum of 25%. The $50 billion financing platform has yielded no results, and parties have requested renegotiation of terms. According to Bloomberg, the $500 billion financing platform launched by Jensen Huang in August, after three months of joint appearances with six major asset management institutions, has yet to finalize any deals. Bloomberg reports that Nvidia previously offered a 25% cap on "residual value support" to the market, but in the past month, some clients and Wall Street partners have demanded a higher guarantee ratio, arguing that Broadcom could offer more generous terms. Even the most optimistic estimates suggest the platform may not announce its first deal until January at the earliest, and this timeline depends on whether Jensen Huang's departure derails negotiations. Against this backdrop, market participants have begun renegotiating terms. Sunaina Sinha Haldea, Global Head of Private Capital Advisors at Raymond James, told CNBC that the management change provides a natural pause for all involved institutions, allowing them to re-examine transaction terms; she expects capital won't withdraw, but "they may demand a higher uncertainty premium," meaning credit spreads across the entire downstream of Nvidia's balance sheet will widen across the board. Saxo's chief investment strategist, Charu Chanana, warned that against the backdrop of ever-expanding debt, revolving financing structures, and uncertain returns already being questioned by the market, the greater risk lies in the ripple effect of AI financing—"This is not yet a financing crisis, but it could become a catalyst for the repricing of risks in the AI ​​ecosystem." "The deer dies under the hunting light": Kress takes over a slowing machine. According to the Wall Street Journal, in August of this year, Jensen Huang summoned key financial executives to his office to confront a growing problem: Nvidia was negotiating billions of dollars in guarantees for companies that simply could not afford its chips. Some of the deals were spearheaded by Nico Caprez, Huang's son-in-law and a vice president promoted in January. He promised emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that Nvidia could arrange credit support within weeks in exchange for a share of their revenue, and dozens of companies flocked to the deal. At this very meeting, Huang publicly criticized Kress's presentation, interrupting her and calling her "a deer in the headlights," criticizing her as merely a reporting CFO rather than an executive capable of defining strategy—the very role the company's board has now decided to give her. However, historically, Kress has been one of the few executives throughout the expansion frenzy who consistently questioned "how much are these guarantees really worth?" According to reports from The Wall Street Journal, Reuters, and The Information: it was she who halved OpenAI's initial commitment; it was she who tried behind the scenes to curb Caprez's trading impulses; and it was she who raised questions that no one was willing to answer in the frenzied atmosphere—how to screen deals, how to price guarantees, and how to calculate returns. In October of this year, Nvidia began to gradually tighten its financing tap, requiring approval from its executive team and board of directors for every new deal. However, external pressure is coming from multiple directions simultaneously—the U.S. Department of Justice is investigating customer chip shipments, the chairman of a House committee is demanding closed-door briefings, and the position of the company's permanent chairman remains vacant. The fragile chain of emerging cloud service providers: the first wave of shocks from guarantee repricing. The reason Nvidia's guarantees are so valuable is that they can package borrowers with low credit quality as investment-grade debt issuers. Goldman Sachs' analytical framework shows that in CoreWeave's deferred withdrawal term loan structure, the customer's credit rating directly determines how much debt the SPV can bear and at what interest rate it can finance. When Nvidia's credit endorsement filled the rating gap, the previously junk-rated emerging cloud service provider was able to finance at investment-grade rates. According to The Information, Nscale secured $860 million in rental guarantees for its Texas site and is negotiating over $5 billion in credit support from Nvidia for its West Virginia campus built for Anthropic—and Nvidia's guarantee is a prerequisite for Nscale to complete its financing. "If capital providers now believe that Nvidia's guarantees are no longer worth the price they were a week ago, those emerging cloud service providers will be in crisis," an insider told Fortune. Goldman Sachs' "Top of Mind" report also included Chamath Palihapitiya's pessimistic assessment of emerging cloud service providers: these companies have a break-even utilization rate of around 70% to 75%, while currently they are generally in a gray area of ​​75% to 85%—in this range, they are profitable, but the profits are insufficient to pay off their debts before the hardware becomes obsolete. Nothing needs to get worse; this outcome will naturally follow. The signs are already emerging. Australia's Firmus first scaled back and then withdrew its IPO plans in October, and CoreWeave's euro bonds are still trading at around 80 cents. Once Nvidia truly tightens its guarantees, the first to be impacted will be the borrowers with the heaviest debt burdens. On Tuesday, November 17th, Kress will host Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call as interim CEO and CFO. Analysts will undoubtedly press her about the $500 billion figure. Her response will reveal to the market whether "Nvidia Bank" remains open for business or has quietly shifted to a maintenance-oriented approach for existing loans.

data.title: Grayscale: The market is breaking free from BTC dominance; Vitalik Buterin: ETH should focus on value storage.
data.description:
Golden Weekly is a weekly blockchain industry summary column launched by Golden Finance, covering key news, market and contract data, mining information, project updates, and technological advancements.

Bitcoin

Bitcoin mining difficulty is expected to decrease by about 7.8% this weekend, the largest drop since June

On November 12th, according to Mempool data, Bitcoin mining difficulty will see a decrease of about 7.8% this weekend, the largest difficulty drop since June.

The market is hotly debating the fact that the US spot Bitcoin ETF has seen net outflows of $2.35 billion for two consecutive weeks.

The US spot Bitcoin ETF has seen net outflows for two consecutive weeks, with a cumulative size of $2.35 billion.

The US spot Bitcoin ETF has seen net outflows for two consecutive weeks, with a cumulative size of $2.35 billion.

... From November 9th to 13th, net outflows totaled $1.07 billion, following a net outflow of $1.28 billion the previous week. On Friday, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a single-day net outflow of $185.4 million, with BlackRock IBIT experiencing a net outflow of $143.5 million and Fidelity FBTC a net outflow of $41.9 million. This marks the seventh consecutive trading day of net outflows for US spot Bitcoin ETFs, with a cumulative net outflow of approximately $1.71 billion since November 5th. BlackRock IBIT has experienced net outflows for 11 consecutive trading days, with a cumulative outflow of approximately $2.35 billion. Since November, the fund has seen net outflows of $2.12 billion, accounting for approximately 90% of the total net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs during the same period. The underlying reason, according to some, is that some miners are shutting down their mining equipment and redirecting electricity and data center resources to AI computing power businesses. The reduced difficulty means a lower barrier to entry for mining blocks, which will improve the unit computing power revenue for the remaining online miners. Hackers are offering TSMC employee data for 3 Bitcoins; TSMC confirms some employee information leak. On November 12th, Jiemian News reported that hackers were offering what appeared to be TSMC employee data on an underground forum, claiming it contained 46,000 records, a file size of 6.9GB, and asking for 3 Bitcoins (approximately NT$7.4 million). They also stated that if no one buys it within a week, it will be made public. TSMC confirmed that data from some current and former employees was leaked. Preliminary investigations indicate the vulnerability originated from a cloud service provider, and TSMC's internal systems were not compromised. The leaked data does not include production or customer data. The company has notified affected employees and is working with the service provider and investigative agencies to address the issue. On November 12th, according to Lookonchain monitoring, a whale that had been dormant for four years deposited 1,000 BTC, worth approximately $73.78 million, into Binance eight hours prior. US Spot Bitcoin ETFs See Net Outflows of $2.35 Billion for Two Consecutive Weeks. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen net outflows for two consecutive weeks, totaling $2.35 billion. Of this, $1.07 billion flowed out between November 9th and 13th, following a net outflow of $1.28 billion the previous week. On Friday, US spot Bitcoin ETFs experienced a single-day net outflow of $185.4 million, with BlackRock IBIT seeing a net outflow of $143.5 million and Fidelity FBTC seeing a net outflow of $41.9 million. This marks the seventh consecutive trading day of net outflows for US spot Bitcoin ETFs, with a cumulative net outflow of approximately $1.71 billion since November 5th. BlackRock IBIT has seen net outflows for 11 consecutive trading days, accumulating approximately $2.35 billion in outflows. Since November, the fund has experienced net outflows of $2.12 billion, accounting for about 90% of the total net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs during the same period. Grayscale: The crypto market is gradually moving away from Bitcoin dominance, and the correlation between returns across different sectors continues to decline. On November 13th, Grayscale released a research report pointing out that over the past three years, Bitcoin price changes have only explained about 50% of the return differences across various sectors of the crypto market, with the remaining changes largely influenced by sector and specific asset factors. At the same time, the correlation between different crypto sectors has fallen from its previous high, and market performance is gradually diverging. Data shows that Bitcoin's actual volatility over the past year was approximately 43%, while the annualized volatility of the cryptocurrency payment sector was 49%, and the AI ​​sector reached as high as 85%. Grayscale believes that as the crypto market matures, investors can expect to obtain more diversified sources of returns through different sectors and asset allocations, but decreased correlation does not necessarily mean reduced investment risk. Ethlabs proposes a 2027 goal for Ethereum to achieve quantum-resistant and AI-resistant upgrades, and plans to adjust the Hegotá hard fork roadmap. Ethlabs published an article on the Ethereum community forum proposing to advance the goal of achieving post-quantum resistance and post-AI attack resistance for Ethereum to 2027, codenamed "pqai27," and suggesting that it be listed as the highest priority in protocol development. The team believes that AI is accelerating the solving of mathematical problems and the discovery of software vulnerabilities, and the timeline for quantum computing threats is also advancing. Ethereum needs to improve the long-term security of the network by adopting cryptographic schemes with fewer security assumptions, strengthening client security, and formal verification. To advance this goal, Ethlabs recommends reassessing the scope of the subsequent hard fork Hegotá, reconsidering features not part of the pqai27 critical path, and announcing the withdrawal of QuickSlots resources previously secured for Hegotá, which will be instead invested in pqai27. The initial roadmap envisions include: implementing a quantum-resistant consensus mechanism and account signature scheme in the Hegotá phase, enabling Ethereum to operate with quantum resistance; subsequently, achieving full-capacity operation through signature aggregation and quantum-resistant data availability schemes. Ethlabs emphasizes that achieving "pqai-ready" by 2027 is the core objective, while achieving full-capacity "pqai-scaled" is a more challenging extended goal. Ethereum Foundation-affiliated wallet sells another 1,000 ETH, worth approximately $2.03 million. On November 11th, according to Lookonchain monitoring, the Ethereum Foundation-affiliated wallet (0x5CBC) sold another 1,000 ETH, worth approximately $2.03 million, 9 hours ago. An ancient ETH whale appears to have sold 7,507.52 ETH in the past 9 hours, with an estimated profit of $15.93 million. According to on-chain analyst @ai_9684xtpa, an ancient whale that bought 37,000 ETH at $1.50 each back in 2015, appears to have sold 7,507.52 ETH in the past 9 hours, with an estimated profit of $15.93 million. This whale has transferred $28.54 million worth of ETH (12,163.52 ETH) to exchanges since September 29th, with an average deposit price of $2,346.87. If sold, the return would be a staggering 156,358%. The funds can be traced back to August 2015, originating from ShapeShfit. On November 8th, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin stated that rather than positioning ETH as a fee-burning token, its value storage function should be emphasized. He argued that the fee-burning narrative is not as powerful as it seems, and optimizing around this goal may struggle to balance decentralization and anti-capture capabilities; a value storage positioning aligns with Ethereum's decentralized advantages, and its stability has real value for asset holders. He supports retaining EIP-1559 and its burning mechanism, but believes that even if the fee burning remains below 10% of the break-even point for an extended period, there is no need to be disappointed. A wallet that had been dormant for over two years withdrew approximately 34,601 ETH from Binance in the past three hours, worth approximately $73.75 million. The original article did not disclose the wallet's identity or the reason for the withdrawal. Other Projects OpenAI Shifts to General AI Models for Direct Robot Control, No Longer Developing Dedicated Models. On November 14th, according to Fortune magazine, OpenAI has disbanded its independent robotics research team and reassigned related researchers to other departments within the company. OpenAI stated that this move is not an abandonment of its robotics business, but rather an attempt to accelerate the development of general-purpose robots. Following the adjustment, robotics researchers will be integrated into the core research team led by Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams will be transferred to the applications department headed by President Greg Brockman. This adjustment reflects a shift in OpenAI's strategic direction: the company believes that general-purpose AI models can be directly applied to robot control, eliminating the need to develop separate robot AI models. OpenAI claims that cutting-edge general-purpose models, including GPT-6 Astra, have demonstrated their capabilities for robot applications. An NVIDIA study showed that agents equipped with Astra achieved a 74.8% success rate in simulated robot operation tests, higher than the 51% previously reported for dedicated robot models on the same leaderboard. OpenAI still plans to develop humanoid robots, with CEO Altman previously stating the goal of conducting the first public demonstration in 2027. However, industry insiders point out that general-purpose models still have limitations such as slower operating speeds and reliance on cloud networks, and robotics companies still have advantages in real-world deployment and data accumulation.

Coinbase CEO: Coinbase Pro Coming Soon, Advancing AI Financial Accounts and US Stock Perpetual Contracts

On November 13th, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong stated that Coinbase stores over 99% of its custodied crypto assets in cold wallets and uses the latest AI models to strengthen defenses, sometimes gaining early access to the models. He stated that Coinbase's security design takes into account the possibility of employees being scammed, and no single person, single computer, or single system can independently transfer user funds. He also mentioned that seven of the world's largest banks have chosen to partner with Coinbase, and Coinbase holds over 80 licenses globally. AI-powered financial agents are a key focus for Coinbase. Armstrong cited predictions that by 2030, the transaction volume processed by AI agents could reach $3 trillion to $5 trillion.

He believes that crypto networks are well-suited as the infrastructure for intelligent agents to execute transactions, and developing financial accounts for AI agents is one of Coinbase's priorities. Regarding stock tokenization, Armstrong stated that tokenized stock trading volume on Coinbase has exceeded $5 billion. He believes that tokenized stocks are more accessible than traditional stocks and can be integrated with DeFi protocols, for example, allowing holders to earn returns on their stock assets. Regarding US stock perpetual contracts, Armstrong stated that Coinbase has been pushing for the compliant implementation of such products in the US for years and welcomes the cooperation between SEC and CFTC officials on this matter. He pointed out that stock perpetual contracts are already traded in markets outside the US. He also teased the upcoming launch of Coinbase Pro, but did not give a specific date in the post. Hyperliquid Protocol Q3 Revenue Reaches $190.9 Million, Up 21.7% Quarter-over-Quarter. According to Hyperliquid Research, on November 13th, the Hyperliquid protocol's revenue reached $190.9 million in the third quarter, a 21.7% increase quarter-over-quarter, marking a new high for a single quarter in 2026. Two new revenue streams contributed the majority of the growth: • USDC Reserve Earnings: $17.3 million since August 27th, accounting for approximately half of the quarterly revenue increase. • Priority Fees: $9.6 million, a 3.3-fold increase quarter-over-quarter; this was due to traders paying more for faster execution and data access. These two revenue streams combined accounted for 14% of the protocol's total revenue in the third quarter and did not require additional trading volume. Robinhood's October crypto transaction volume was $17 billion, a sharp drop of 48% year-over-year. On November 13th, Robinhood released its October crypto transaction data, showing an overall notional crypto transaction volume of $17 billion, a 48% year-over-year decrease and a 21% month-over-month decrease compared to September. By platform, the Robinhood App's crypto transaction volume was $6.8 billion, a 51% year-over-year decrease; its Bitstamp platform's transaction volume was $10.2 billion, a 45% year-over-year decrease. The significant decline in crypto transaction activity has put pressure on its related business revenue. Arthur Hayes: Flop Labs Testnet and Airdrop to Officially Launch on November 24th On November 13th, Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX and CEO of FLOP Labs, announced on the X platform that the Flop Labs testnet and airdrop will officially launch on November 24th, 2026. He stated that if this date is adjusted, the project team will release an updated announcement in advance. Flop Labs is a blockchain project focused on AI intelligent agents, emphasizing a fair issuance model with no private placements or VC funding.

data.title: Unveiling the mastermind behind the assassination of Nvidia's Jensen Huang
data.description:
Author: Liang Yimeng; Source: Nanyang Dream Record

It's no secret that Jensen Huang and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei are openly at odds over AI policy and chip exports. From heated debates in Washington to Huang's public rejection of Amodei's push for a comprehensive export ban, the two have long made their stance clear.

But look at who's suddenly swarming in to oust Huang.
The people at Anthropic overlap with the think tanks, former officials, and forums behind this round of reporting. Its money supports the leading members of Congress who spearhead the attacks. Its funding network built many of the think tanks whose critics came from.
A coincidence is a coincidence.
A string of connections, and that's it. When the people leading the attack on a CEO are all linked to his biggest industry rival, shouldn't these connections be disclosed? Those reporting on this should all be asking: Who benefits? So far, almost no one has asked. How I Started Investigating Initially, I thought it was just a collaboration between China hawks and the media in a midterm election year, targeting Nvidia and Jensen Huang. But the reporting became increasingly strange, some even blatantly racist. So I started following the trail. I started with Ana Swanson, a reporter for The New York Times. She was the first to break the spy story. I wanted to know why such a thin lead deserved so much coverage. I read through her main reports on AI and chips, seeing who repeatedly appeared as a source. Anyone familiar with journalism knows: you won't keep going back to the same person or using their narrative framework unless there's genuine trust between you. One name keeps appearing: Jack Clark, co-founder and head of policy at Anthropic. I. Journalists and Their Sources Clark, a former Bloomberg reporter, later became OpenAI's head of policy. He has a clear understanding of how the media operates. Last May, he gave a pre-dinner talk at an AI policy conference at the Aspen Institute, titled "The Software Singularity." The room was full of people involved in chip and tech geopolitics.

II. Democratic Senators Following the Fire

As soon as the New York Times report was published, Senator Chris Coons immediately jumped in:

"A crazy relationship between the Trump administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires...Congress will launch an investigation."

In July of this year, Coons received $2,500 from Anthropic's corporate political action committee, AnthroPAC. Jack Clark personally donated $5,000 to the committee.
Clark lives and works in San Francisco, while Coons represents Delaware.
This isn't some hometown camaraderie: when Clark testified before the House Intelligence Committee in 2019, he listed his degree as "Varndean College, Brighton" in the UK. Clark also served as a non-resident researcher at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technologies (CSET). Remember that name. III. The Georgetown and CSET Circle Among those who have spoken out the loudest against Jensen Huang, a surprising number are from Georgetown University: Mark Jia, Professor at Georgetown Law School, former Supreme Court Justice Clerk; Ryan Fedasiuk, part-time faculty member at Georgetown, former CSET analyst, publicly demanding Huang's resignation; Dennis Wilder, former CIA official, now teaching at Georgetown. CSET was established in 2019 within Georgetown's School of Foreign Service, researching AI and chip security issues. Its initial funding came from Open Philanthropy, the largest financial backer in the "effective altruism" circle. Co-founder Holden Karnofsky later joined Anthropic. Now let's look at Jia. When the Pentagon listed Anthropic as a "supply chain risk," Lawfare cited his research on the legal boundaries of national security assessments. In other words, when the target is Anthropic, the legal threshold for "national security risk" should be very high. But when the target is Huang Renxun, where does that threshold disappear?

4. "Financial Times"

McGuire has approximately 12,000 followers. What most people haven't noticed is his resume: he served on Biden's National Security Council under Tarun Chhabra, who is now Anthropic's Director of National Security Policy. The two appeared together at the DSET forum in Taipei this June.
Within hours, Representatives Seth Magaziner, Susan Rice, Adam Kinzinger, and Nicholas Kristof all retweeted the post. A post from an account with 12,000 followers has garnered over 9 million views, making it the most viewed post in the entire incident.

VI. Senate Banking Committee

In February of this year, Ahmed met with members of the Senate Banking Committee to push for tighter AI chip exports to China. Shortly afterward, Senators Warren and Banks announced the Senate version of the AI ​​OVERWATCH Act.
Senior Republican Senator Kevin Cramer received $1,000 from AnthroPAC in July. He is now publicly demanding that Jensen Huang resign as CEO.

VII. Money, and Anthropic's Own Board of Directors

During this election cycle, Anthropic is running two money-printing machines:
AnthroPAC (Federal Election Commission number C00946111) directly donates to campaign committees.

$40 million was given to Public First Action, a 501(c)(4) organization with affiliated super PACs. Amody himself added another $1 million. Public First Action ran ads recognizing lawmakers who supported the chip export bill, including House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast. Mast also received $2,500 from AnthroPAC, one of the chairmen who signed the November 4 letter demanding an explanation from Jensen Huang. Now let's look at Anthropic's governance structure. Richard Fontaine is a member of Anthropic's "Long-Term Interest Trust," which determines the majority of board seats. Fontaine is also the CEO of the Center for a New American Security (CNAS), one of Washington's leading think tanks for chip export control policy. The CNAS research on chip smuggling details the same tactics currently being used against Nvidia: targeting shell companies in Southeast Asia and intermediaries in third countries. Fontaine has been in Anthropic's trust since June 2025. The hawks and Anthropic are not just aligned in their positions; they share leadership. One coincidence is one thing, but a whole series? The New York Times reporter who first broke the story of Jensen Huang's espionage? Her long-time source happens to be a co-founder of Anthropic. The Financial Times reporter who championed the "romantic relationship" narrative? He happened to have exclusive access to information about Anthropic cutting off Chinese companies. The person who turned "romantic relationship" into "sleeping with a Chinese spy" on X? He happened to be a former subordinate of Anthropic's head of national security policy. The senator who demanded Jensen Huang's resignation? He happened to be sitting in the very committee that Ahmed had lobbied behind closed doors, and he also received money from the Anthropic Political Action Committee. The House Speaker who signed the joint letter demanding an explanation from Huang? He happened to simultaneously receive support from both the Anthropic Political Action Committee and the organization that received $40 million from Anthropic. A coincidence is a coincidence. A series of coincidences, what do you call it? VIII. The Singapore Statement That Was Collectively "Unseen" First published in the New York Times on October 29, followed by the Wall Street Journal on October 30. The Wall Street Journal stated that Singaporean officials had concerns about Alice Huang and had investigated her ties to China. The next day, the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs issued a formal written statement: "The Singapore government and its officials have not said anything like that. Nor has any such investigation been conducted against Alice Huang." The statement even published the Wall Street Journal's question and the government's response, which made no mention of her. A week later, the story exploded worldwide. These same media outlets, somehow, purely by coincidence, all overlooked the official denial. Nine, From "Spy" to "Extramarital Affair" Five days passed, and still no evidence; the story of the Chinese spy seemed on the verge of falling apart. Then, another coincidence: it suddenly transformed into the story of Huang Renxun's extramarital affair.

It's still the New York Times, only this time, a whole new group of reporters are at the byline. Perhaps that's a coincidence.
Another coincidence: all of this happens right around the time Anthropic launches its approximately $61 billion IPO. This is the second largest IPO in history, and just days before, Nvidia's market value evaporated by more than $500 billion.

Ten, The Last Coincidence Before the IPO: The Benches in Washington

Anthropic has just filled the benches in Washington, with people from both administrations.
From the Biden Administration
Tarun Chhabra: Director of National Security Policy at Anthropic. Former Coordinator for Technology and National Security at the National Security Council.
Ben Buchanan: Now at Anthropic. Former White House AI Advisor, one of the designers of the AI ​​chip "proliferation rule".
Ben Buchanan: Now at Anthropic. Former White House AI Advisor, one of the designers of the AI ​​chip "proliferation rule".
Elizabeth Kelly: Now at Anthropic. Former Director of the U.S. AI Security Institute. Joel Meyer: Responsible for Anthropic's federal civil public sector operations. Former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security, where he established the first AI working group. Benjamin Della Rocca and Kristine Lee: Now at Anthropic. Both were former National Security Council staff members. From the Trump Administration Chris Liddell: Appointed to the Anthropic Board of Directors in February 2026. Former Deputy Chief of Staff at the White House (first term). Sihao Huang: Appointed Director of Frontier Computing Strategy in September 2026. Former Senior AI Policy Advisor at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. Sarah Heck: Policy Director, responsible for communication between Anthropic and the White House. Former National Security Council (first term). Mary Croghan: Anthropic Washington Policy Team. Former White House Cabinet Office (first term).

data.title: How can Crypto rebuild security and trust in the AI ​​era?
data.description:
Author: imToken

For over a decade, the security narrative in the crypto industry has been almost entirely condensed into a classic slogan: "Not your keys, not your coins."

Whether ordinary users or institutional practitioners, there has long been a default linear security logic—as long as you copy down your mnemonic phrase offline, buy a hardware wallet, or entrust your assets to a leading compliant platform, your security is guaranteed.

However, a series of landmark security incidents recently erupting are completely shattering this illusion of single-point defense.

On one hand, attackers are beginning to exploit AI, social engineering, and software supply chain vulnerabilities to bypass traditional security protections and directly infiltrate internal enterprise systems; on the other hand, even cold wallets and hardware wallets, considered relatively secure, may become new entry points for attacks due to issues with internal access control, device circulation, and third-party suppliers.

With AI rapidly transforming attack and defense methods, the security boundaries of the crypto industry are being redefined. From trading platforms to hardware wallet manufacturers, a new consensus seems to be emerging: the competition in crypto security has shifted from who is better at protecting private keys to who can build a more complete, verifiable, and resilient security system. First, private keys are important, but no longer everything. Looking back at past security incidents in the crypto industry, the most common risks are private key leaks, stolen mnemonic phrases, phishing websites, and smart contract vulnerabilities. These problems haven't disappeared, but attackers are seeking more sophisticated and covert entry points, especially with the rapid proliferation of AI tools, leading to a shift in traditional security boundaries. The Binance security incident on October 29th is a typical example of this change. According to Binance's preliminary investigation, attackers gradually infiltrated the wallet development team's working environment through a tampered software installer, fake job interviews, and malicious code. They then used infected employee devices and internal AI tools to further obtain credentials with container deployment permissions, ultimately accessing the wallet's signature service and initiating unauthorized on-chain transactions. The entire process lasted several months and involved multiple stages, including social engineering, software supply chain, employee terminals, and internal permissions. The attackers did not directly compromise Binance's wallet system; instead, through a multi-stage penetration chain, they gained a springboard to access the company's internal systems and critical permissions. This also illustrates that attackers don't necessarily need to directly obtain the private key; as long as they can abuse the access permissions to critical signature services, they can still cause serious asset losses. Even if the private key is protected using MPC (Multi-Party Computation) fragmentation, it doesn't mean the entire signature system is inherently secure. MPC addresses how to distribute and manage keys and how to complete a signature without fully reconstructing the private key, but it doesn't automatically address who has the authority to initiate a signature, which authorizations can be executed, and how abnormal authorizations can be revoked promptly. In other words, key security and access control are two sets of protection mechanisms that need to be in place simultaneously. Taking the Ledger incident as another example, its chip, operating system, and servers were not compromised. The problem occurred during the distribution process after the device left the manufacturer's control, meaning users could still be attacked during the purchase and initialization stages. Looking at these incidents together reveals a common trend: attackers are increasingly inclined to exploit trust relationships between different systems, rather than simply looking for isolated technical vulnerabilities. This also means that the crypto industry needs to redefine security boundaries, shifting from protecting single assets to protecting the entire asset lifecycle; from focusing on the security of a particular device or system to examining the complete trust chain between people, software, devices, and permissions. However, it's worth noting that the industry hasn't stopped at discussing risks in the face of these changes. II. From Binance to Ledger: How is the Crypto Industry Upgrading its Security Defenses? Following a series of recent security incidents, trading platforms, hardware wallet manufacturers, security agencies, and regulatory bodies have all begun to make adjustments in their respective areas. Looking at these actions together, several noteworthy changes are occurring in crypto security. 1. Binance and Coinbase: From Protecting Keys to Protecting the Entire Signature and Fund Flow Process After the Binance incident, the platform rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tools in a new environment, replaced relevant employee devices, disabled affected credentials and access tokens, and conducted further security checks on employee terminals. Meanwhile, Binance has also strengthened risk control and AI-driven anomaly detection for its wallet service, and plans to introduce an independent security agency to further review the cause of the incident, internal permissions, and related protection systems. These measures, seemingly scattered, actually address the same problem: Once an attacker has gained access to the internal system, how can they be prevented from using their existing privileges to access higher-risk assets? A similar approach can be found in Coinbase's newly released asset protection system. On November 4th, Coinbase published an article specifically introducing its customer asset security architecture, stating that over 99% of customer assets are currently stored in cold wallets, and disclosing a complete set of fund flow control mechanisms. For example, at the key management level, Coinbase employs a distributed key protection mechanism to avoid single-point exposure of private keys; during cold and hot wallet transfers, it sets strict limits on transfer speed and amount, and identifies suspicious operations through abnormal behavior monitoring. These also provide a valuable example: where assets are stored is important, but who can initiate transfers, under what conditions signatures are allowed, and whether operations can be stopped promptly in case of anomalies also determine the overall security level of the system. This is precisely the core logic of Defense in Depth. No single link is assumed to be absolutely secure; on the contrary, even if an employee's device is compromised or a certain permission is abused, other protective mechanisms should still be able to limit the further spread of the attack. 2. Ledger and Trezor: Security Extends to Production, Distribution, and Delivery The changes in the hardware wallet sector are also representative. Following this hardware implantation incident, Ledger began adjusting its device management requirements for authorized distributors, requiring authorized dealers and retailers to suspend sales in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, and to conduct device sampling and inventory checks. Simultaneously, Ledger further clarified that dealers must not resell returned devices, even if the packaging appears intact; devices should not continue to be displayed on open shelves or in showrooms, but should be stored in back-end storage areas and delivered only when a user purchases them. These measures also demonstrate that the boundaries of hardware security are expanding, essentially reducing the opportunities for attackers to access and modify devices. Trezor's adjustments are even more direct. On November 12, Trezor released its latest investigation results, confirming that three Trezor Safe 5 devices sold through the implicated reseller CryptoBilis contained implanted hardware. Simultaneously, Trezor announced it had reduced its authorized reseller network by approximately 80% and required remaining partners to comply with stricter rules regarding procurement, warehousing, and device access management. At the product level, Trezor released firmware version 2.13.1 on November 11, adding protective measures against the discovered implanted module, preventing it from continuing to read screen information. This reflects a shift in hardware security governance: security is no longer solely determined by product reliability at the time of manufacture, but also by the manufacturer's ability to continuously manage supply chain risks and provide effective detection, remediation, and user recovery measures after issues occur. For wallet manufacturers, this means managing not only chips and firmware, but also the entire product lifecycle. 3. From CZ's Security Alliance Initiative to Regulatory Efforts: Industry Collaboration is Taking Shape Beyond internal security upgrades, another noteworthy area is cross-platform collaboration. Following the Binance incident, CZ publicly called for the crypto industry to establish a security alliance to promote security intelligence sharing, cross-security audits, and more efficient tracking and emergency response to stolen funds. This reflects a long-standing contradiction in the crypto industry: while blockchain assets can flow rapidly across platforms and chains, security defenses are often fragmented among different exchanges, wallet manufacturers, security companies, and on-chain analytics firms. The discovery of an abnormal address by one platform does not mean that other platforms can immediately identify it; the discovery of new attack characteristics by one security team does not mean that the entire industry can update its protection strategies in a timely manner. This reflects a defense model different from the traditional enterprise-built security team: connecting the security research, threat monitoring, and incident response capabilities scattered across different organizations, allowing attack information to be identified, shared, and utilized more quickly. Of course, cross-platform collaboration does not mean that all enterprises should unconditionally share internal system information or have the power to arbitrarily freeze user assets. Establishing clear boundaries between security intelligence sharing, trade secret protection, and user asset autonomy also requires further refinement. However, it's clear that crypto security is gradually shifting from relatively isolated corporate self-protection to collaborative defense involving security agencies, platforms, and the community. It's worth noting that after the Binance incident, the Korean Financial Services Commission (FSC) urgently convened the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Security Service, and major virtual asset trading platforms to inspect the exchanges' asset custody and security measures. One key focus was re-evaluating the proportion of assets held in cold wallets on exchanges. According to Korea's current Virtual Asset User Protection Act, exchanges are required to store at least 80% of the economic value of user assets in cold wallets. However, following this incident, regulators further required exchanges to consider increasing the proportion of cold wallets, while strengthening 24/7 deposit and withdrawal monitoring, reserve fund management, wallet signature approval, and administrator access control. This indicates that regulators are beginning to realize that exchange security cannot rely solely on post-incident compensation; it also requires proactive asset isolation and operational restrictions to minimize the losses caused by a single attack. III. In the AI ​​Era, What New Security Standards Do Crypto Products Need? Connecting these recent industry actions reveals a gradually forming more complete security logic. Binance is restructuring its internal systems and permissions, Coinbase is emphasizing multi-layered signature control, Ledger and Trezor are tightening their supply chains, the entire industry is promoting cross-platform emergency collaboration, and South Korean regulators are further strengthening 24/7 monitoring and incident accountability. imToken believes that future crypto products need to rebuild their security systems from at least the following aspects: 1. From Private Key Security to End-to-End Permission Security Private keys remain the core of digital asset security, but they should not be the entirety of the security system. For trading platforms, it is necessary to protect keys, signature services, administrator accounts, development environments, and production deployment permissions simultaneously; for wallet products, it is necessary to clearly distinguish between different stages such as key management, transaction construction, transaction authorization, and final signing. Especially after AI Agents begin to integrate with wallets, trading accounts, and on-chain applications, permission management will become even more important. An Agent that can read market data and check balances should not inherently possess the permission to transfer assets; an Agent that can help users construct transactions does not mean that it can directly complete signing without additional authorization. A reasonable design should include: allocating the minimum permissions according to task requirements, separating querying, transaction construction, transaction approval, and final signing; setting independent confirmation mechanisms for high-risk operations, such as out-of-band confirmation, Passkey, or multi-authorization; all authorizations should have clear scope, validity period, and revocation mechanisms; and retaining verifiable audit logs for critical operations. In short, **AI can help users accomplish more tasks, but it cannot gain unrestricted control over assets.** This is not only a security requirement for AI agents but also a permission standard that the entire crypto product industry needs to establish in the future. 2. From One-Time Audits to Continuous Verification In the past, many crypto products were accustomed to proving their security to users through smart contract audits, code reviews, or hardware security certifications. While these efforts are important, the problem is that audits typically only cover a specific time period, a specific code version, and a specific scope. Passing a smart contract audit for a product does not guarantee that subsequent code upgrades are problem-free; passing chip security tests for a hardware wallet does not guarantee it will not be tampered with during warehousing and transportation. Therefore, future security systems need to shift from one-time audits to continuous verification. 3. From Single-Point Protection to Defense-in-Depth No single technology can solve all security problems. MPC can reduce the risk of single-point key leakage, but cannot automatically prevent incorrect authorization; cold wallets can reduce the risk of remote attacks, but cannot completely eliminate internal operational and supply chain risks; hardware wallets can isolate private keys, but cannot identify all malicious transactions for users. Therefore, a truly mature security architecture requires different layers of protection mechanisms to complement each other. For example, at the identity layer, anti-phishing authentication methods are used to reduce the risk of account and employee credentials being stolen; at the permission layer, least privilege, temporary authorization, and multi-person approval are adopted to prevent a single identity from having complete control; at the device layer, terminal security, hardware integrity verification, and trusted startup mechanisms are strengthened; at the transaction layer, transaction content is simulated, risks are identified, and clearly displayed to prevent users from completing signatures without understanding the transaction intent; at the asset layer, cold wallets, MPC, multi-signature, limits, and anomaly monitoring are used to reduce the possibility of funds being transferred in one go; and at the response layer, emergency suspension, permission revocation, event notification, and cross-platform collaboration mechanisms are established. 4. From "Trusting Brands" to "Security Can Be Verified" For ordinary users, security faces a long-standing problem: information asymmetry. Users often struggle to understand how a wallet manages its private keys, cannot directly assess the legitimacy of an exchange's internal permissions, and are unlikely to personally inspect the hardware wallet's chip, firmware, and supply chain. Therefore, security products cannot rely solely on brand reputation or marketing slogans to build trust. The future lies in making security mechanisms as transparent and verifiable as possible. For example, trading platforms need to continuously disclose asset reserves, custody structures, and key security mechanisms; wallet vendors need to disclose private key management principles, code audit status, vulnerability response processes, and version update records; hardware wallet vendors need to allow users to verify the origin of devices, firmware integrity, and official sales channels. 5. Returning to User Asset Control: The Value and Responsibility of Non-Custodial Wallets After discussing so many security mechanisms, there is another question worth reconsidering: If exchanges, wallet vendors, hardware devices, and third-party services can all become entry points for attacks, how should ordinary users choose their asset management methods? This is also the long-standing value of non-custodial wallets; compared to centralized trading platforms, the core difference of non-custodial wallets lies in asset control. In centralized trading platforms, users typically need to go through the platform's account system, internal wallet system, and the platform's signature process to complete asset transactions. User asset security depends not only on their own account protection but also on the platform's internal permissions, custody architecture, employee management, and operational mechanisms. In non-custodial wallets, users manage their own private keys or mnemonic phrases. The wallet service provider does not directly control the transfer of user assets. Structurally, this means **removing a trusted intermediary for asset custody**, reducing the custody risks associated with the platform holding user assets centrally. However, this does not mean that non-custodial wallets are immune to all attacks. Users can still encounter phishing websites, malicious contracts, false authorizations, device infections, and mnemonic phrase leaks, requiring users to pay greater attention to their key management and transaction security. Therefore, for non-custodial wallets like imToken, what truly deserves continuous development is further improving the security experience throughout the entire usage process, centered around user autonomy. This also reflects a more comprehensive security philosophy. From Binance's internal access breach to Ledger and Trezor's hardware supply chain risks, and exchanges' re-evaluation of cold wallet ratios, recent events remind us that the standards upon which the crypto industry has built security and trust in the past need further upgrading. Private keys remain important, but they are no longer everything. Future security competition will occur simultaneously across multiple levels, including cryptography, software supply chains, AI access control, hardware design, asset custody, and incident response. For the entire industry, rebuilding trust cannot be accomplished with a single security audit, a proof of reserves, or a simple statement that "user assets are unaffected." Security is a prerequisite for trust, but verifiable, sustainable, and accountable security is the true infrastructure the crypto industry needs to build to move towards the next stage.

data.title: Democrats set their sights on Silicon Valley: Who's next after Jensen Huang?
data.description:
Author: Bitpush

Jensen Huang's sudden departure may only be the beginning of a concentrated outbreak of political risks at US tech giants.

On November 12, Nvidia (NVDA) announced that its founder, Jensen Huang, had resigned as CEO and board member, with CFO Colette Kress temporarily taking over. Since the cheating scandal broke, Nvidia's stock price has fallen by nearly 20%, and the resignation news further shook Wall Street.

This crisis coincides with a major shift in the US political landscape.

In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democratic Party gained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. With the new Congress set to take office in January 2027, the close relationship between tech giants and the Trump administration is becoming a key area of ​​investigation for the Democrats.

Which key figures are at play in this?

On November 13, according to financial media Semafor, AI security organizations such as Guardrails Action sent a letter to Democratic congressional leaders Schumer and Jeffries, urging them to hold hearings on the Jensen Huang incident and strengthen oversight of the Trump administration's AI policies. In fact, an investigation has already been launched. On November 12, Democratic Senators Ron Wyden and Richard Neal formally requested the Department of Commerce to preserve all records of Nvidia's chip export approvals, tariff arrangements, and communications with Huang. These two senators are not ordinary members of Congress. Ron Wyden is the senior Democratic leader of the Senate Finance Committee, having served as its chairman. He has long been involved in the formulation of U.S. tax, trade, and foreign economic policies. He is also a key figure in U.S. internet privacy and digital rights legislation. Richard Neal is the ranking Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee and a former chairman. This committee holds significant authority over federal tax and trade legislation. The collaboration between the two means the investigation is not limited to Nvidia alone, but delves into the Trump administration's trade and tariff decision-making process. The core of the controversy is the Trump administration's arrangement in December 2025 to allow Nvidia to export H200 chips to China, while simultaneously imposing a 25% tariff on related imports. Two lawmakers questioned whether this practice turns national security reviews into a tool for the government to obtain commercial revenue. Another noteworthy figure is Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren.

Warren is currently the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee. She was a key advocate for the design of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and is known for holding large banks and financial institutions accountable.

During the Wells Fargo fake accounts scandal in 2016, Warren sharply questioned the bank's CEO, John Stumpf, at a congressional hearing. Stumpf ultimately resigned.

This experience has made her a well-known political figure on the issue of accountability for American corporate executives. It's worth noting that Warren has also worked closely with Republican Senator Jim Banks on the issue of chip exports. In May of this year, Banks introduced the AI ​​OVERWATCH Act, which Warren supported along with Republican Senator Tom Cotton and others. This bill aims to further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips from the United States. When the Democratic and Republican hawks on China stand together, the political pressure on Nvidia is no longer determined by any single party. The pressure even extends to within the Trump administration. Reuters reports that senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Lutnick should resign. Lutnick has been criticized for failing to promptly restrict some companies suspected of transshipping advanced chips to China. However, White House officials say Trump still trusts him. Next Targets: Musk, Meta, Apple The Democratic investigation will clearly extend beyond Nvidia. On November 6th, The Washington Post exclusively revealed that Democrats are preparing for a congressional investigation in early 2027, with Musk's companies, Meta, and Apple among the initial targets. Musk may face the most complex political scrutiny. Democrats plan to investigate whether the Trump administration used its AI chatbot Grok to participate in military operations planning in Venezuela, while also focusing on Musk's previous involvement with the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and the relationship between his business interests and government decision-making. Meta (META) is under scrutiny for signing confidentiality agreements with local governments during its data center development. With the surge in demand for AI computing power, data center power consumption, financial incentives, and local environmental issues are becoming bipartisan political controversies. The investigations facing Apple (AAPL) include its tracking app related to immigration enforcement and its relationship with the White House. One of the main drivers of these investigations is Representative Robert Garcia. Garcia is currently the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and is expected to become the committee's chair if Democrats gain control of the House in 2027. The House Oversight Committee's role is to investigate potential problems in federal government agencies, the use of public funds, and government operations. The committee can hold public hearings, request documents, and, with appropriate authorization, issue legally binding subpoenas. According to information released by the committee's Democratic wing, since Garcia became the ranking Democrat in July 2025, the committee has pushed for several subpoena actions with bipartisan support. Besides AI security, government-business relations are another area where Democrats can more easily win voter support. On November 5th, Senator Richard Blumenthal requested several technology companies to submit documents related to donations to Trump's White House banquet hall; Nvidia, Apple, Meta, Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and Amazon (AMZN) were among those on the list. Blumenthal is currently the ranking Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. This subcommittee, part of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, focuses on government operations, corporate behavior, and potential abuses of power. He is expected to chair the subcommittee after Democrats take control of the Senate in 2027. According to an investigation by The Washington Post, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million, while federal government contractors such as Microsoft and Palantir (PLTR) also donated significantly. Other publicly traded companies that received the document requests include Salesforce (CRM), Cisco (CSCO), Micron Technology (MU), and Booz Allen Hamilton (BAH). What Washington is truly concerned about is whether these companies, while donating, simultaneously received regulatory licenses, policy preferences, or contractual benefits from the federal government. For the Democrats, who are about to gain congressional investigative power, donation documents, administrative decision-making records, and testimony from corporate executives are all sources of evidence to investigate potential conflicts of interest. A shift in public opinion, with anti-tech giants becoming a new political tool. A key context for the Democrats' increased emphasis on technology regulation at this time is the changing attitudes of voters. An NBC News/SSRS exit poll for the 2026 midterm elections showed that 90% of voters considered government corruption a significant or key factor influencing their votes, slightly higher than the 89% who cited the cost of living as a significant factor. A CNBC poll of 1,000 people conducted from October 14-18 showed that 93% of respondents opposed elected officials personally holding or trading federal contractor stock, and 89% opposed businesses owned or invested in by immediate family members of the president receiving federal government contracts. These figures provide political impetus for Democrats to scrutinize government-business relations. CNBC reporter Steve Liesman, discussing the aftermath of the Jensen Huang scandal on MS NOW, stated that tech executives may reduce high-profile public interactions with the White House in the future to mitigate political risk. Meanwhile, a number of political lobbying groups are actively pushing Democrats to take a tougher stance. Over the past few years, a number of organizations have gradually emerged in the United States that specialize in researching AI risks, promoting legal regulation, and engaging in political lobbying. These organizations are not government departments and cannot directly enact laws, but they can influence Congressional agendas through policy research, media outreach, public mobilization, and election funding. Among them, The Tech Oversight Project is particularly active. Founded by Sacha Haworth, this organization has long advocated for stronger antitrust, privacy, and cybersecurity regulations for large technology platforms such as Google, Meta, and Apple. Haworth herself has extensive experience in Democratic politics, having served on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) and the House Majority PAC, and has also participated in anti-Trump election campaigns. On November 11, she issued a memo demanding that the new Congress hold hearings for tech company CEOs as soon as possible after taking office to investigate political donations, AI security, and data center costs. Furthermore, over 50 organizations, including Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI), Demand Progress, and Encode, jointly called on Democrats to appoint members of Congress who support mandatory AI regulation to chair key committees. Technology regulation is evolving from a professional policy issue into a crucial political tool for the Democratic Party to vie for votes. Does Wall Street need to reassess the risks? For investors, the policy environment for the US AI industry is changing. In the short term, Nvidia and Commerce Secretary Lutnick face the most direct pressure from investigations; at the corporate level, Musk's companies, Meta, and Apple are the priority targets explicitly named by the media. In the long term, the scope of regulation may expand further. Democratic members of the House of Representatives have jointly demanded that Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX report on AI model security incidents. Microsoft, Amazon, and large data center operators may also be included in electricity cost and infrastructure regulations. However, although the Democrats control both houses of Congress, they still lack the votes needed to overturn the president's veto. Therefore, what is most likely to emerge first in early 2027 is not comprehensive regulatory legislation, but rather congressional hearings, subpoenas, accountability for corporate executives, and bipartisan push for chip export restrictions. The policy easing environment enjoyed by US tech giants over the past two years may be approaching a turning point. The political chain reaction triggered by the Jensen Huang incident may be the starting point for the next regulatory cycle in the US AI industry. For Wall Street, while the growth prospects of AI are important, future valuations may no longer be determined solely by computing power demand and profit growth, but also by the reshaping power relationship between tech giants and Washington.

data.title: Goldman Sachs 2027 Equity Outlook: AI Capital Expenditure Peaks, Earnings Growth Slows Significantly
data.description:
Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

Goldman Sachs' 2027 Global Equity Strategy points out that the AI ​​capital expenditure boom is nearing its peak, and global profit growth will slow significantly. S&P 500 profit growth is expected to drop from 36% to 11%, with depreciation pressure gradually emerging. However, cloud giants' valuations have corrected to a forward P/E ratio of 19.7, lower than the consumer staples sector, and are characterized as "relatively defensive" assets. Goldman Sachs forecasts a target price of 8700 for the S&P 500, recommending an overweight position in the US and Japan, and an underweight position in Europe.

As the AI ​​capital expenditure boom nears its peak, the engine of global stock market profit growth is slowing down. In its latest 2027 Global Equity Strategy Outlook, Goldman Sachs points out that although profit growth will slow significantly, growth stocks currently being sold off by the market—especially US hyperscale cloud computing companies—now possess investment value.

In his latest report, "Finding Value in Growth," Goldman Sachs' Chief Global Equity Strategist, Peter Oppenheimer, points out that valuations of AI-related companies have significantly corrected, reflecting market concerns about peaking AI capital expenditures and slowing returns, providing investors with an attractive entry point. Cloud giants are currently trading at a forward P/E ratio of 19.7, not only below the lower end of their historical 20-year range but also below the 21.0 of the consumer staples sector. Goldman Sachs characterizes them as "relatively defensive" assets. This outlook comes against the backdrop of the Nasdaq 100 index experiencing its worst single-day drop since the COVID-19 pandemic, and Nvidia also plummeting this week due to news of its founder and CEO's departure. Goldman Sachs predicts a 12-month target price of 8700 for the S&P 500, representing a roughly 14% increase from current levels. The Japanese TOPIX index and Asian markets have the greatest potential upside, while Europe is expected to underperform with an estimated return of only about 6%. 2026: Earnings Drive the Index, Valuations Cool Down. The Oppenheimer team's core assessment for 2026 is three key words: effective diversification, earnings bearing the main driving force for growth, and valuation corrections across all markets. Over the past 12 months, the pattern of US stocks consistently outperforming the market from 2009 to 2025 has reversed, with total returns across regions becoming relatively similar. However, the underlying drivers differ. In Asia, excluding Japan and emerging markets, 12-month forward EPS contributes approximately 70%, while valuation compression drags down returns by over 50%. The sources of profit growth are mainly threefold: continued compound growth in the technology sector; rising oil prices boosting the profits of commodity producers; and the spillover effect of the technology capital expenditure boom driving HALO industries, namely "asset-intensive, low-failure-rate" industries, such as the industrial sector. Meanwhile, valuations have not continued to expand. The S&P 500 has fallen from near the 100th percentile of its 20-year range to a P/E ratio of 18.5; the MSCI AC World currently has a forward P/E ratio of 15.6 and a PEG ratio of 1.1, close to its 35-year average. This is also the starting point for subsequent allocation judgments: the index is not cheap enough to be at crisis levels, but compared to the previous high valuation phase, the risk-reward ratio has changed. Regarding the 12-month target, the S&P 500 target is 8700 points, corresponding to a 14% increase. Regionally, the TOPIX index in Japan and Asia have the largest upside potential, while Europe lags behind, with only 6%. Profits "Halved": AI Capital Expenditure Begins to Ebb, Depreciation Pressures Take Center Stage. Goldman Sachs warns that in 2027, profit growth in almost all major markets will slow significantly. Specifically, S&P 500 profit growth is expected to fall from 36% to 11%; the pan-European CSI 600 from 18% to 7%; the TOPIX from 24% to 9%; and Asia's from nearly 80% to less than 30%. This is what is known as a "halved" profit growth. The core reason lies in the slowdown in capital expenditure growth for hyperscale cloud service providers, while depreciation from previous investments begins to materialize. Goldman Sachs estimates that cloud giants' capital expenditures contributed 12 percentage points to S&P 500 EPS growth this year, up from 5 percentage points in 2025 and 2 percentage points in 2024; however, this contribution will drop to 9 percentage points by 2027, and by 2028, it will become a drag of 5 percentage points. The industry is also cooling down simultaneously. Information technology profit growth will slow from nearly 90% to 45%; communication services will shift from 34% growth to a 5% decline; the energy sector, which saw 99% profit growth this year amid the Iran war, is expected to contract by about 10% afterward; and the materials sector will slow from 45% to 12%. The only sector expected to accelerate is healthcare, but this sector has already undergone a valuation reassessment. This means that those who previously benefited from the AI ​​capital expenditure boom—such as chipmakers, industrial companies, and energy equipment manufacturers—will begin to face slower growth. Meanwhile, the "buyers" of capital expenditures, namely US cloud giants, have been repositioned in a relatively defensive framework due to their declining valuations. Goldman Sachs believes that AI-related companies have already undergone a significant valuation correction, reflecting market concerns about the peak of AI capital expenditures and a slowdown in investment returns. However, this decline has actually created a new investment window. Recently, value stocks have significantly outperformed growth stocks across all regions, with the valuation gap between value and growth narrowing from over 100% at its 2021 peak to approximately 45% to 50%. At the same time, the value factor is approaching the 90th percentile of its 20-year range, historically more expensive than growth. The global technology sector is at the 20th percentile of its 20-year range, with its price-to-earnings ratio close to that of the value factor. The most crucial pricing signal has emerged from the US cloud giants: these companies currently have a forward P/E ratio of 19.7, lower than their 20-year range and lower than the 21.0 of the consumer staples sector. The valuation premium of the top five US stocks relative to the remaining 495 stocks has also largely converged, unlike the extremes seen at the peaks of 2000 or 2021. This is the basis for the view that "cloud giants are defensive growth assets": valuations have come down, balance sheets remain relatively healthy, and revenue streams are more diversified. The net debt-to-equity ratio for the technology sector in developed markets is in the single digits, while the overall market is around 50%. Chips, storage, and hardware: Greater upside potential, but also greater volatility. The report points out that the most "high-risk, high-return" opportunities are concentrated in strong cyclical growth sectors such as semiconductors, storage, and hardware. Goldman Sachs Asia strategists estimate that current share prices in the South Korean memory sector imply a 70% downward revision of consensus earnings for 2027, which Goldman Sachs considers "seemingly overly pessimistic," given company disclosures that their DRAM and HBM products are sold out until 2029. The sector is currently trading at 0.7 times its 2028 price-to-book ratio, a level Goldman Sachs notes "historically foreshadows strong future returns." However, Goldman Sachs maintains a neutral rating on the Asian market due to concentration risk: South Korea and Taiwan together account for approximately 50% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, the information technology sector has a weighting of over 40%, and the three "AI core stocks"—TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix—each individually account for approximately 30%. This widens the price-to-earnings discount of emerging markets relative to developed markets to approximately 50%, the widest since at least 2010. Goldman Sachs forecasts a 17% return on the US dollar in Asia (MXAPJ), but maintains a neutral stance after adjusting for volatility (24.2% annualized volatility). Yields and Oil Prices: Key Assumptions Under Challenge. The third pillar of Goldman Sachs' 2027 strategy is the expectation of low oil prices and declining bond yields. Goldman Sachs' commodities team expects Brent crude to fall from around $100/barrel at the end of 2026 to $78/barrel at the end of 2027, and anticipates the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank to shift to rate cuts "around the end of 2027." Goldman Sachs' interest rate forecasts are "still more dovish than market pricing." However, the reality differs significantly from these expectations. Currently, the 10-year US Treasury yield is at 5.12%, having climbed further last Thursday after two consecutive releases of better-than-expected CPI data; Goldman Sachs' own economists have just revised their forecasts to a later rate cut. Regarding oil prices, Brent crude rebounded 3.3% to around $96 last Thursday after Trump stated that the US does not need a deal with Iran, and the "normalization" of the Middle East situation remains a matter of prediction. In terms of regional allocation, Goldman Sachs ultimately recommended overweighting the US and Japan, neutral Asia and emerging markets, and underweighting Europe.
